idiom_name: CryptoKit (Apple platforms) / swift-crypto: AES.GCM, SymmetricKey, Keychain
implementation_notes: Swift's platform answer is CryptoKit, whose documentation states the posture directly: "Prefer CryptoKit over lower-level interfaces. CryptoKit frees your app from managing raw pointers, and automatically handles tasks that make your app more secure, like overwriting sensitive data during memory deallocation." The realization is therefore: use its published constructions (AES.GCM, ChaChaPoly, SHA256, HMAC, Curve25519) with SymmetricKey, store keys in the Keychain or Secure Enclave rather than source or UserDefaults, and rely on server-side enforcement rather than hidden client logic. The classic violation in this ecosystem is the secret compiled into the app bundle: the binary is on the attacker's device, so an embedded API key or private client scheme is public by construction.
pitfalls: Secrets in the bundle: API keys, tokens and "private" algorithm constants in Resources, Info.plist or code are extractable from the IPA; client code must assume the attacker can read it.
Dropping to CommonCrypto/pointer-level code when CryptoKit provides the high-level construction reproduces exactly the errors CryptoKit exists to prevent (its documentation's own rationale).
Keys stored in UserDefaults or plists instead of the Keychain (Secure Enclave for high-value keys) are readable from backups and device dumps.
